questions.question: How does method chaining work in Ruby?
questions.title: Method Chaining in Ruby
questions.direct_answer: Method chaining sends the next method to the value returned by the previous method. In `'  ruby  '.strip.upcase`, `strip` returns `'ruby'`, then `upcase` runs on that result. A chain works only while each return value supports the following call, so return types and possible `nil` values matter more than the visual dots.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand chaining as a left-to-right pipeline where each method returns the value the next needs (strings, arrays, relations).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Chaining a method that returns nil (chain breaks), or expecting mutation from a non-! method.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Chaining calls methods left to right, each returning the value the next needs: 'hello'.upcase.reverse. Works for strings/arrays/relations. Non-! methods return new values; ! methods mutate.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Each method in a chain receives the previous method's return value.
- Read `'x'.strip.upcase` from left to right as a value pipeline.
- Know each return type; a `nil` result can stop the next call.
- Bang does not mean 'chainable'; some `!` methods return `nil` when unchanged.
- Split a long chain when naming an intermediate step improves meaning or debugging.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Method chaining calls the next method on the value returned by the previous method. Ruby evaluates `'  ruby  '.strip.upcase.reverse` from left to right: `strip` returns `'ruby'`, `upcase` receives that String and returns `'RUBY'`, and `reverse` receives that result and returns `'YBUR'`. It is ordinary method dispatch, not a separate pipeline feature.

A chain works only while each result responds to the next message. `sort` and `uniq` return Arrays, so `[3, 1, 2, 2].sort.uniq.first` is valid; `first` then returns one element or `nil`. Before adding another call, check that return type and whether absence is possible. The same-looking dot can cross from String to Array, Hash, one object, or `nil`.

A bang suffix does not promise a chainable return. Several String bang methods, including `downcase!`, return `nil` when no change was needed. A search such as `find` may also return `nil`. Safe navigation with `&.` is useful when missing data is an allowed outcome; it should not hide an unexpected absence that the program ought to report.

Keep a chain when the steps are short, their return values are clear, and the left-to-right flow explains the operation. Name an intermediate value when one stage can fail, needs inspection, or represents an important business concept. Eager collection chains may also allocate intermediate Arrays; a lazy Enumerator helps with very large or endless inputs, but eager code is usually clearer for a small collection.

support.title: Inspect successful and missing chain results
support.code:
puts '  ruby  '.strip.upcase.reverse
p [3, 1, 2, 2].sort.uniq.first

word = 'ready'
p word.downcase!

profiles = []
name = profiles.find { |profile| profile[:active] }&.fetch(:name)&.upcase
p name
support.caption: Output is YBUR, 1, nil, and nil. The last two chains stop because their method contracts allow absence.

sections.title: The receiver and result at each step of a method chain
sections.content:
The only reliable way to reason about a chain is to write the return value under each call. A transformation such as `strip` returns a String, so another String method can follow. `map` returns an Array, `group_by` returns a Hash, `first` returns one element or `nil`, and `each` usually returns the original receiver. The visible syntax looks uniform even though those contracts differ.

Mutation adds another distinction. A method ending in `!` conventionally has a more dangerous counterpart, often because it changes the receiver, but Ruby does not promise that every mutating method has a bang or that every bang method returns `self`. Several String bang methods return `nil` when no modification was required. Chaining through that conditional result is fragile.

Safe navigation, `account&.owner&.name`, stops and returns `nil` when its receiver is `nil`. It should represent an allowed missing relationship, not silence an unexpected bug. If absence needs a default, an explicit `fetch`, `||`, or branch can explain that policy more clearly.

Eager collection stages can allocate one intermediate Array per transformation. `(1..).lazy.map(...).select(...).first(5)` changes evaluation: values flow through the pipeline only until five matches are found. Use that when size justifies it; for a small Array, the eager chain is usually simpler.

sections.title: Every return value becomes the next receiver
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["'  ruby  '"] -->|strip returns String| B["'ruby'"]
  B -->|upcase returns String| C["'RUBY'"]
  C -->|reverse returns String| D["'YBUR'"]
  N[method may return nil] -.->|next call cannot run| X[NoMethodError]
```

sections.title: Expand a chain to inspect its contracts
sections.content:
```ruby
result = '  ruby  '.strip.upcase.reverse
# => 'YBUR'

step_1 = '  ruby  '.strip     # String: 'ruby'
step_2 = step_1.upcase        # String: 'RUBY'
step_3 = step_2.reverse       # String: 'YBUR'

numbers = [3, 1, 2, 2]
numbers.sort.uniq.first       # => 1

word = 'ready'
word.downcase!                # => nil, because nothing changed
# word.downcase!.reverse      # would call reverse on nil

profile = nil
profile&.fetch(:name, nil)&.upcase # => nil when absence is allowed
```
